sources.title: Diataxis: the compass
findings: Two questions place content: does it inform action or cognition, and does the reader acquire or apply it.
The answers map to tutorial, how-to guide, reference, or explanation, and apply to a whole page or a single sentence.
sources.limits: A framework from one author; the page itself says to apply it loosely.

sources.title: Diataxis: how-to guides
findings: A how-to guide serves a competent reader with a goal and is distinct from a tutorial, which teaches.
Explanation and reference stay out of the guide and are linked instead; the title says exactly what the guide shows.

sources.title: Diataxis: reference
findings: Reference only describes: facts without instruction, opinion, or explanation, structured like the product.
Generated reference can stay accurate to the code but is not all the documentation a product needs.

sources.title: Documenting Architecture Decisions
findings: An ADR has a title, context, decision, status, and consequences, runs one to two pages in prose, and lives in the repository under sequential, never-reused numbers.
A reversed decision stays in place and is marked superseded with a pointer to its replacement; ADRs cover architecturally significant decisions.
sources.limits: The original lightweight form; later templates add fields.

sources.title: Technical Writing One: Audience
findings: Name the reader roles and how close each is to the knowledge, then write what they need to learn or do minus what they already have.
Experts skip explanations newcomers need (curse of knowledge).
sources.limits: A course for engineers; guidance, not measured effect.

sources.title: Technical Writing Two: Large documents
findings: Choose one long document or short linked ones by reader and content type; the introduction states coverage, prerequisites, and non-coverage.
Background such as history belongs at the end, linked; headings name the reader's task.
sources.limits: A course for engineers; guidance, not measured effect.

sources.title: Technical Writing One: Define your document's scope and audience
findings: State the scope and the non-scope readers would expect, and declare the audience and prerequisites.
Put the key points first, since some readers stop after the opening; in review, cut what does not serve the scope.
sources.limits: A course for engineers; guidance, not measured effect.

sources.title: Docs as Code
findings: Documentation is written with the code's tools: version control, plain text, code review, automated checks, and the issue tracker.
Teams can block feature merges that lack documentation, so it is written while the feature is fresh.
sources.limits: A community guide; the page does not describe staleness checks in detail.
